  "explanation": "X and Y are double first cousins (they share both grandparent pairs). Their children P and Q therefore share both great-grandparent pairs, making them second cousins with doubling. Hence the most precise label is \"double second cousins.\"",
  "answer": "D",
  "choices": [
    "A) First cousins",
    "B) Second cousins",
    "C) Third cousins",
    "D) Double second cousins"
  ]
}

{
  "topic": "Blood Relations and Family Trees",
  "question": "Using standard English kinship terms only (in-law limited to spouse, spouse’s parents/siblings, siblings’ spouses, children’s spouses), R is married to S, S’s brother is T, T’s wife is U, and U’s brother is V; who is V to R?",
  "explanation": "R→S (spouse) →T (sibling-in-law) →U (that sibling’s spouse) →V (that spouse’s sibling). This passes beyond immediate in-law scope and never introduces a blood link. Thus V has no standard direct kin term to R.",
  "answer": "C",
  "choices": [
    "A) Brother‑in‑law",
    "B) Cousin-in-law",
    "C) No standard direct relation (affinal chain only)",
    "D) Nephew-in-law"
  ]
}

EXAMPLE RESPONSE:
{
  "topic": "Blood Relations and Family Trees",
  "question": "In a single breath: let P and Q be, respectively, the child of the only brother of R’s mother and the child of the only brother of R’s father; if one selects either P or Q and calls that person S, then S is who to R?",
  "explanation": "Whether S is the child of R’s maternal uncle or paternal uncle, S is the child of a parent’s brother. That relation to R is always a first cousin.",
  "answer": "B",
  "choices": [
    "A) Nephew/Niece",
    "B) First cousin",
    "C) First cousin once removed",
    "D) Not uniquely determinable"
  ]
}

EXAMPLE RESPONSE:
{
  "topic": "Blood Relations and Family Trees",
  "question": "“Pointing to a man, I say: \"He is the only son of my mother, I am the only daughter of my mother, and I have no brothers\"; under the standard meaning of \"only\" and monogamy, who is he to me?”",
  "explanation": "“If I have no brothers, then my mother has no sons. That directly contradicts \"He is the only son of my mother.\" The constraints cannot all hold; the scenario is impossible.”",
  "answer": "C",
  "choices": [
    "A) Brother",
    "B) Cousin",
    "C) Configuration impossible under the constraints",
    "D) Nephew"
  ]
}

  "topic": "Blood Relations and Family Trees",
  "question": "Using standard English kinship, with no adoption and monogamy allowed but remarriage permitted: \"Z is the spouse of the parent that my spouse shares with their sibling\"; who must Z be to me?",
  "explanation": "The shared parent is my parent‑in‑law. That parent’s spouse could be my other parent‑in‑law (if still married to the other biological parent) or a later spouse (step‑parent‑in‑law). Both occur; only the A/B indeterminacy is guaranteed.",
  "answer": "D",
  "choices": [
    "A) Parent-in-law (mother-/father-in-law)",
    "B) Step-parent-in-law (spouse of a parent-in-law who is not my spouse’s parent)",
    "C) No relation",
    "D) Not uniquely determinable between A and B"
  ]
}

  "topic": "Blood Relations and Family Trees",
  "question": "A and B share exactly one parent (are half-siblings), each has one child (X is A’s child, Y is B’s child), there are no other intermarriages; what is the precise relation between X and Y?",
  "explanation": "Children of half-siblings share a single grandparent rather than a full pair. The precise term is \"half-first cousins\"—not full first cousins (which require both shared grandparents) and not second cousins.",
  "answer": "A",
  "choices": [
    "A) Half-first cousins",
    "B) First cousins",
    "C) Second cousins",
    "D) Not determinable"
  ]
}
